# Limits, open questions, and directions {#sec-limits}

ISLA has no measured accuracy advantage over GeoTransolver or plain
Transolver once every model receives the freestream at the same unit
scale. Against the baselines as their recipes ship them, fed the physical
freestream velocity, ISLA was several times more accurate at a few dozen
HiLiftAeroML training cases; against the same baselines fed the unit
direction that ISLA receives, it is 1.1–1.25x *less* accurate at 35 cases
(1.07–1.11x against the weights-off ablation, not adopted; @sec-part-baseline), and the
same holds at every rung re-measured so far: baselines ahead at 210 cases
(GeoTransolver 0.83x), at four geometries (0.76x) and at the fixed angle
(0.78x), and between parity and ahead at 21 geometries (0.92x). What
stands is parity with GeoTransolver at full HiLiftAeroML data and, at full
DrivAerML data in float32, 10% behind the unit-drive GeoTransolver and 8%
behind Transolver (7% and 5% for the weights-off ablation, not adopted), a lead on
interior velocity (25% in float32, three seeds) with deficits on interior
pressure (8%) and eddy viscosity (27%), and
a set of contracts that GeoTransolver does not have. This chapter states
the boundary of each claim as a fact about the evidence, lists the open
questions with the preregistered outcome that settles each, and names what
would change the recommendation.

## What is established {#sec-established}

Eight results are settled to the standard of the fair-comparison protocol
(@sec-protocol), and together they support the one-sentence verdict of
@sec-verdict: no measured accuracy advantage over input-matched baselines;
a contribution of contracts, and an interior lead pending its control. Each
carries its numbers and its own scope statement in its home section; this
chapter adds only the limits.

- At 35 HiLiftAeroML training cases, GeoTransolver and Transolver fed the
  unit freestream direction are more accurate than ISLA (baseline ÷ ISLA
  0.90 and 0.83; lower on 130 and 152 of 180 cases), and the 2.8x deficit
  of the physical-velocity baselines was an artifact of the comparison
  protocol, not of the architectures (@sec-part-baseline). Every other
  HiLiftAeroML ratio in @sec-data-efficiency is a physical-drive
  measurement whose unit-drive rerun is not yet measured.
- On DrivAerML, GeoTransolver is 1.2–1.3x more accurate from 27 cars up
  (@sec-de-drivaerml), measured with GeoTransolver's physical-velocity
  input, so that lead is a lower bound.
- Full-data accuracy on HiLiftAeroML (parity against the physical-drive
  GeoTransolver) and on DrivAerML (@sec-full-data).
- The pose contract: rotation and translation covariance exact by
  construction, with a finite-precision residual on the bf16 path that is
  measured rather than assumed (@sec-pose, @sec-mt2-contracts).
- Learning-rate robustness, and the memory and step-time measurements of
  both models in one harness (@sec-mt2-cost).
- Sampling-density robustness of ISLA with the similarity gauge, and the
  failure of the constant-gauge configuration without it
  (@sec-robustness-density).
- Interior accuracy: ISLA with query tokens and the signed distance leads
  GeoTransolver's volume configuration on interior velocity by 27% at a
  third of the parameters and trails on pressure (6%) and eddy viscosity
  (27%) in float32; the passive, query-independent decode trails it by 3.1x
  (float32; @sec-interior).
  GeoTransolver-volume consumes the physical freestream velocity (38.9 m/s)
  where ISLA consumes the unit direction; retrained with the unit direction
  it changes by under 2% on every field, so the ordering stands
  (@sec-nb-udrv-int-verdict).
- Regime extrapolation: nothing tested generalizes across a flow-regime
  boundary (@sec-regime-extrapolation).

## Limits of each headline claim {#sec-review-honesty}

### The HiLiftAeroML ladder: what its curves measure {#sec-limits-data-efficiency}

**The ladder's GeoTransolver and Transolver curves are physical-drive
measurements over 35 to 1,260 training cases on HiLiftAeroML; their
unit-drive counterparts exist at 35 cases only, and there they lie below
ISLA's curve.** The quantity throughout is the surface-pressure relative L2
error as defined in @sec-metrics, averaged over the 180 validation cases
shared by every rung of the nested splits. The log-log slope of a segment
is −Δ log(error)/Δ log(cases) between adjacent rungs; a larger slope means
error falls faster with data. Fitted on the two-seed means, the
physical-drive GeoTransolver's slope is 0.50 from 35 to 210 cases and 0.74
from 210 to 1,260; ISLA's is 0.43 and then 0.25 (on the three-seed means
GeoTransolver's segments are 0.553 and 0.675;
results/hilift_slopes_threeseed_2026-09-08.json). The physical-drive
GeoTransolver steepens as data grows and ISLA flattens; a naive power-law
extrapolation of the two curves puts GeoTransolver at 0.015 and ISLA at
0.029 at 5,000 cases, a factor of two in GeoTransolver's favour. With the
unit direction as input GeoTransolver scores 0.111 (0.124 at 1e-3) and
Transolver 0.115 at 35 cases (@sec-part-baseline), already below ISLA's
0.138 (0.123 in the weights-off ablation), so the
unit-drive curves start below ISLA's and their shape above 35 cases is not
yet measured (@sec-program-status). Every seed at a rung trains on the same
curated subset, so the seed bands measure initialization, not the choice of
training cases; the curves are one draw of each training set.

```{python}
#| label: fig-slope-extrapolation
#| fig-cap: >
#|   The ladder's curves and the unit-drive points. Pressure relative L2
#|   error on the shared 180-case HiLiftAeroML validation set versus number
#|   of training cases, log-log, seed means (small dots are the two seeds)
#|   for GeoTransolver with the physical freestream velocity as input (red)
#|   and ISLA (blue); the Transolver control with the physical velocity, at
#|   its better learning rate (grey, dashed), is shown at the two rungs it
#|   was run on. Hollow markers at 35 cases are GeoTransolver (red) and
#|   Transolver (grey) fed the unit freestream direction, everything else
#|   unchanged; they are the valid comparison with ISLA at that rung and lie
#|   below it. Each solid segment is labelled with its log-log slope. The
#|   dotted lines extend the last measured segment of each solid curve as a
#|   power law to 5,000 cases; they are the naive extrapolation, not a
#|   prediction, and the grey band marks the region with no measurements.
#|   How to read this: the solid red and grey curves measure the
#|   physical-drive protocol, not the baselines' data efficiency; the
#|   unit-drive curves above 35 cases are not yet measured. Protocol:
#|   learning rate 1e-3 for GeoTransolver and ISLA, 3e-3 for Transolver, 500
#|   epochs, bf16, no augmentation, 10,000 sampled points per case, two
#|   seeds. Data: results/hilift_ladder_reduction_2026-09-03.json,
#|   results/t1_transolver_control_reduction_2026-09-05.json and
#|   results/udrv_reduction_2026-09-09.json.
#| code-fold: true
import json, math, statistics
from pathlib import Path
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib as mpl
# book palette (mirrors figures.py without importing it: that module
# switches matplotlib to Agg, which suppresses inline output here)
BLUE, RED = "#2a78d6", "#e34948"
INK, INK2, MUTED, GRID, BASELINE = "#0b0b0b", "#52514e", "#898781", "#e1e0d9", "#c3c2b7"
mpl.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110, "font.size": 10, "axes.edgecolor": BASELINE,
                     "axes.labelcolor": INK2, "axes.grid": True, "grid.color": GRID,
                     "xtick.color": MUTED, "ytick.color": MUTED, "xtick.labelcolor": INK2,
                     "ytick.labelcolor": INK2, "axes.spines.top": False,
                     "axes.spines.right": False, "legend.frameon": False})

lad = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "hilift_ladder_reduction_2026-09-03.json"))
t1 = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "t1_transolver_control_reduction_2026-09-05.json"))
rungs = [(35, "lad_hl_{a}_super_scarce_seed{s}"), (210, "lad_hl_{a}_scarce_seed{s}"), (1260, "{a}_hl_lr1_seed{s}")]
curves = {}
for arch in ("gt", "mt2"):
    xs, means, pts = [], [], []
    for n, pat in rungs:
        v = [lad[pat.format(a=arch, s=s)]["pressure_l2"] for s in (42, 43)]
        xs.append(n); means.append(statistics.mean(v)); pts.append(v)
    curves[arch] = (xs, means, pts)
# Transolver at its better learning rate per rung (3e-3 at both rungs run).
txs, tmeans, tpts = [], [], []
for n, pat in [(35, "t1_hl_transolver_super_scarce_{lr}_seed{s}"), (210, "t1_hl_transolver_scarce_{lr}_seed{s}")]:
    best = min(([t1[pat.format(lr=lr, s=s)]["pressure_l2"] for s in (42, 43)] for lr in ("lr1e3", "lr3e3")),
               key=statistics.mean)
    txs.append(n); tmeans.append(statistics.mean(best)); tpts.append(best)
# Unit-drive baselines at 35 cases (the valid comparison at that rung).
udrv = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "udrv_reduction_2026-09-09.json"))["arms"]
gt_unit_35 = udrv["gt_unit_35"]["seed_pressure"]
tr_unit_35 = udrv["transolver_unit_35"]["seed_pressure"]

X_EXTRAP = 5000
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 5.0))
ax.axvspan(1260, 8000, color=GRID, alpha=0.35, lw=0, zorder=0)
ax.text(1260 * 1.06, 0.5, "no measurements", color=MUTED, fontsize=8.5, va="top")
ax.plot(txs, tmeans, color=INK2, ls="--", lw=1.4, marker="^", ms=6, zorder=3)
for x, v in zip(txs, tpts):
    ax.scatter([x] * 2, v, color=INK2, s=12, zorder=4)
# Transolver label to the right of its 210-case point (clear of both solid curves)
ax.annotate("Transolver", (txs[1], tmeans[1]), xytext=(8, 0), textcoords="offset points",
            color=INK2, fontsize=9.5, ha="left", va="center")
style = {"gt": (RED, "GeoTransolver", "o"), "mt2": (BLUE, "ISLA", "s")}
for arch, (xs, means, pts) in curves.items():
    c, name, mk = style[arch]
    up = arch == "gt"  # GeoTransolver slope labels above its curve, ISLA below
    ax.plot(xs, means, color=c, lw=2.2, marker=mk, ms=7, zorder=3)
    for x, v in zip(xs, pts):
        ax.scatter([x] * 2, v, color=c, s=14, zorder=4)
    for i in range(2):  # slope label per measured segment
        slope = -math.log(means[i + 1] / means[i]) / math.log(xs[i + 1] / xs[i])
        xm, ym = math.sqrt(xs[i] * xs[i + 1]), math.sqrt(means[i] * means[i + 1])
        ax.annotate(f"slope {slope:.2f}", (xm, ym), xytext=(0, 9 if up else -11),
                    textcoords="offset points", color=c, fontsize=9, ha="center",
                    va="bottom" if up else "top",
                    bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.12", fc="white", ec="none", alpha=0.85))
    # naive power-law extrapolation of the last measured segment
    s_last = -math.log(means[2] / means[1]) / math.log(xs[2] / xs[1])
    y_ext = means[2] * (X_EXTRAP / xs[2]) ** (-s_last)
    ax.plot([xs[2], X_EXTRAP], [means[2], y_ext], color=c, ls=":", lw=1.6, zorder=2)
    ax.scatter([X_EXTRAP], [y_ext], color=c, s=28, facecolors="white", zorder=4)
    # ISLA (upper endpoint) labelled above its point, GeoTransolver (lower) below
    ax.annotate(f"{name}\nnaive extrapolation {y_ext:.3f}", (X_EXTRAP, y_ext),
                xytext=(8, -6) if up else (8, 6), textcoords="offset points", color=c,
                fontsize=9, ha="left", va="top" if up else "bottom")
    # architecture names: GeoTransolver above its 35-case point, ISLA below-left of its 210-case point
    if up:
        ax.annotate(name, (xs[0], means[0]), xytext=(0, 12), textcoords="offset points",
                    color=c, fontsize=10.5, fontweight="bold", ha="center", va="bottom")
    else:
        ax.annotate(name, (xs[1], means[1]), xytext=(-8, -6), textcoords="offset points",
                    color=c, fontsize=10.5, fontweight="bold", ha="right", va="top")
# unit-drive baselines at 35 cases: hollow markers, named in the legend
handles = []
for v, c, mk, name in ((gt_unit_35, RED, "o", "GeoTransolver, unit drive (35 cases)"),
                       (tr_unit_35, INK2, "^", "Transolver, unit drive (35 cases)")):
    m = statistics.mean(v)
    ax.scatter([35] * 2, v, s=14, facecolors="white", edgecolors=c, zorder=4)
    handles.append(ax.scatter([35], [m], s=60, facecolors="white", edgecolors=c,
                              marker=mk, lw=1.8, zorder=5, label=name))
ax.legend(handles=handles, loc="lower left", fontsize=9, title="hollow: unit-drive input",
          title_fontsize=9, alignment="left")
ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xticks([35, 210, 1260, 5000]); ax.set_xticklabels(["35", "210", "1,260", "5,000"])
ax.set_yticks([0.01, 0.02, 0.04, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4]); ax.set_yticklabels(["0.01", "0.02", "0.04", "0.10", "0.20", "0.40"])
ax.set_xlim(14, 8000); ax.set_ylim(0.009, 0.7)
ax.set_xlabel("Training cases [count]  (HiLiftAeroML nested splits)", color=INK2)
ax.set_ylabel("Pressure error\nrel-L2 [–]", color=INK2, rotation=0, ha="right", va="center", labelpad=28)
ax.set_title("Physical-drive ladder curves with naive power-law extrapolation,\nand the unit-drive baselines at 35 cases (180-case validation set)",
             color=INK, loc="left", fontsize=10.5, pad=10)
ax.grid(True, which="major", color=GRID); ax.grid(False, which="minor")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Three facts bound what the curves can say. The measurements are scoped to
the range in which every production CFD dataset in this program lives; no
scaling-law statement is made. ISLA's flattening may be a floor of the
protocol rather than a property of ISLA: at 1,260 cases the two
architectures share 70% of their residual on identical points, the
correlation between two-seed disagreement and per-case error collapses for
both, and accuracy still rises with points per case (6,500 → 10,000 points
is worth 8% for ISLA), which is what a resolution or label floor looks like
(@sec-shared-floor). And the baselines' curves are not their data
efficiency: a unit-drive GeoTransolver that starts at 0.111–0.124 rather than
0.381 at 35 cases has a different curve, whose shape decides whether ISLA
is behind at every rung or only at the smallest; the reruns at 210 and
1,260 cases and on the geometry rungs (@sec-open-questions) are what would
settle it, and none is yet measured (@sec-program-status).

### The HiLift accuracy figures are validation-set figures {#sec-limits-validation}

**Every HiLiftAeroML accuracy number in this book is scored on the shared
180-case validation set; the 360-case test set has not been spent on the
accuracy claims, and no HiLiftAeroML split remains that could confirm them
independently of the program's own history.** The protocol evaluates the
final-epoch checkpoint of every run, so no checkpoint is selected on
validation error. The validation set entered more than one decision: each
architecture's learning-rate choice on the full 1,260-case split
(@sec-lr-protocol), Transolver's learning-rate choice per small-data rung,
the design of the ablations that followed earlier readouts, and the choice of
which results to present. The ladder therefore carries no checkpoint-selection
optimism, but the learning rates were chosen on the same 180 cases (118
geometries) the ladder is scored on, and every control, ablation and
stratified readout in @sec-data-efficiency reads the same cases. The test
splits were spent only on regime extrapolation and the raw-coordinate
discriminator (@sec-regime-extrapolation, @sec-limits-regime), which train on
different splits. Those two evaluations, however, read 900 and 723 cases
that between them contain every one of the 180 geometries, and the
manifests overlap: the 360-case data-efficiency test set shares 179 cases
with them, the geometry test set 182 and the deflection test set 182, and
the latter two also share 37 and 40 cases with the validation set
(@sec-splits; results/hilift_exposure_ledger_2026-09-08.json). Every
remaining test split is therefore *held out per checkpoint*, since no model
trained on it, but not a *program-level confirmation*, since results on
overlapping cases have already informed the program's decisions; and
removing the already-read cases post hoc would define a new, selected
population, not a replacement confirmatory set. A sealed evaluation of the
35-case ISLA and unit-drive baseline checkpoints on the 360 test cases would
still be informative as a within-protocol held-out check of the 0.90 and
0.83 ratios (@sec-part-baseline), and is not yet measured
(@sec-program-status); an independent confirmation needs geometries no part
of the program has scored, which on HiLiftAeroML means a prospective
dataset.

### The mechanism question: answered at 35 cases, open above it {#sec-limits-mechanism}

**The carrier of the physical-drive gap at 35 cases is identified, and it
sits on the baseline side of the protocol: the magnitude of the freestream
input. Nothing in ISLA carries an advantage at that rung, because with the
input matched there is no advantage to carry** (@sec-part-baseline). The
search of ISLA for the ingredient remains informative about ISLA. Five
single-factor ablations at 35 cases (adding raw coordinates, which breaks
the SE(3) contract; replacing the invariant seeds by raw vectors; turning
the similarity gauge on; turning the measure weights off; removing the
relational routing from the encoder) each changed its error by between
−12% and +16% (@sec-mechanism), so no single contract or channel is
load-bearing for ISLA's own accuracy, and the exactness of the SE(3)
contract neither costs nor buys anything measurable in distribution. Those
are measurements of ISLA and they stand. What they were meant to explain
does not: against the unit-drive baselines ISLA's 0.138 is 1.25x behind
GeoTransolver's 0.111 (1.1x behind its 1e-3 lane, 0.124) and 1.2x behind
Transolver's 0.115; the weights-off ablation (0.123, not adopted) is 1.11x
and 1.07x behind.

On DrivAerML, where the geometry variation is a smooth morph of one car,
the same ladder protocol at a frozen learning rate of 3e-3 for both
architectures gives GeoTransolver the lead: the two are tied at 14 cases
(GeoTransolver/ISLA 0.99) and GeoTransolver is 1.2–1.3x more accurate than
ISLA at every rung from 27 to 218 cases (@tbl-drivaerml-dataeff-ladder in
@sec-data-efficiency), with the physical velocity (38.9 m/s) as its input. At
435 cars the unit-drive rerun changes nothing (0.0503 against 0.0498 in
float32, 0.0556 against 0.0548 in bfloat16, inside the null band;
@sec-nb-uw-verdict, @sec-nb-fp32-drivaer-regrade), so on DrivAerML the physical
input was not a handicap and the small-data ladder's ordering is expected
to stand; the ladder's unit-drive reruns are not scheduled.

Every other mechanism measurement that compared ISLA with a baseline on
HiLiftAeroML compared it with a physical-drive baseline, and each is a
measurement of that protocol until its unit-drive rerun is measured
(@sec-program-status). On the fixed-angle split (126 geometries at 12°,
validated on 18 geometries never seen at any angle) ISLA scores 0.036
against 0.179 for the physical-drive GeoTransolver (5.0x, 18 of 18
geometries) and 0.091 for the physical-drive Transolver (2.55x); the
unit-drive reruns of both baselines reverse the ordering, 0.029 and 0.032,
each ahead of ISLA on 18 of 18 geometries (@sec-nb-udrv-single-verdict), so
the fixed-angle rung is measured and ISLA is behind. On the
unseen-geometry ladder ISLA scores 0.250 against the physical-drive
GeoTransolver's 0.449 from four training geometries (1.8x; 172 of 180
cases, which are 18 geometries at ten angles, so the geometry is the
independent unit and the case count is descriptive;
results/hilift_paired_stats_geometry_2026-09-08.json) but 0.250 against
the unit-drive GeoTransolver's 0.189 (ratio 0.76 by the mean; 9 of 18
geometries each way; @sec-nb-udrvl-geo40-verdict), and 0.102 against the
physical-drive 0.143 from 21 geometries (1.40x) but 0.101 against the
unit-drive GeoTransolver's 0.093 (ratio 0.92; GeoTransolver lower on 136 of
180 cases; @sec-nb-udrvl-geo210-verdict). The observation behind those numbers,
that ISLA's error responds to the number of training geometries while the
physical-drive GeoTransolver's does not (0.38 → 0.45 and 0.14 → 0.14 as the
geometries fall from 33 to 4 and from about 126 to 21), is a fact about a
model whose per-case error at 35 random cases was nearly case-independent
(coefficient of variation 0.15) and whose input scale had collapsed its
global-context routing; a unit-drive GeoTransolver is not geometry-blind
(0.189 at 4 geometries, 0.093 at 21, against 0.449 and 0.142 with the
physical drive), which the reruns at 4 and 21 training geometries
measured. The transplant test (GeoTransolver and Transolver at 35 cases with
n·d, r̂·d and |r|/L appended to their per-cell inputs, physical velocity
kept) moved Transolver from 0.402 to 0.297 and GeoTransolver not at all
(0.392 to 0.394); it appended features to a mis-scaled input and could not
have found the input. The mixed-angle control for the fixed-angle split
(physical-drive GeoTransolver 0.226 against ISLA 0.077, 3.0x) and the
decomposition of the fixed-angle gap into a part that separates the two
baselines and a part common to both are physical-drive measurements of the
same kind.

What the reruns decide is stated in advance (@sec-nb-udrvl-prereg). If the
unit-drive baselines match or beat ISLA at every rung, the mechanism
question is closed because there is nothing to explain, and ISLA's standing
on surface pressure is parity to behind on both datasets. If ISLA keeps an
advantage at some rung (baseline ÷ ISLA at least 1.10 with ISLA lower on at
least two thirds of the cases, and on at least 12 of 18 geometries on the
geometry rungs), that rung and its mechanism become the program's only
accuracy claim, stated against the unit-drive baseline, and the
localization and perturbation follow-ups of @sec-open-questions run there.

The DrivAerML shortfall, in turn, is not located anywhere on the car. The
natural hypothesis is that ISLA lacks the global context a bluff body's
wake demands: the rear surfaces' pressures are set by separated flow, so
ISLA's error should concentrate there relative to GeoTransolver's. Binning
each validation case's 10,000 points into streamwise thirds and taking the
per-bin RMS pressure-error ratio ISLA/GeoTransolver (medians over the 48
cases, two seed pairs), the rear third reads 1.27 and 1.32 against the
front third's 1.16 and 1.28; the rear-to-front factor is 1.10 and 1.03,
at or under the preregistered falsification bar of 1.1
(results/drivaer_station_attribution_2026-09-07.json; @sec-nb-drivaer-station-verdict).
Both models put about 56–59% of their squared error on the front third and
about 20% on the rear; ISLA is uniformly a little worse everywhere, and
least worse on the middle third (1.10, 1.12). Like the physical-drive
GeoTransolver's error on high-lift geometries (@sec-mechanism), the gap is
case-level, which points to fit rather than a missing physical channel: a
wake-context
extension would be aimed at a deficit the data do not show. Width alone does
not close it either: an ISLA with hidden width 256 instead of 192 scores
0.062 on the same validation set against 0.063–0.067 for the reference width
and 0.053 for GeoTransolver
(results/mixedres_training_2026-07-31/sweep/mega_reduction.json). And the two architectures agree on which cars are hard: their per-case
errors are rank-correlated at 0.86–0.89, the same as each model with its
own second seed (0.87), and the per-case ratio sits between 1.11 and 1.38
for 80% of cars, with GeoTransolver ahead on 47–48 of 48
(results/drivaer_percase_correlation_2026-09-07.json). The gap is a
near-constant factor on a shared difficulty ordering, and every
GeoTransolver number in it was produced with the physical-velocity input.

The same localization instrument was applied to HiLiftAeroML with a
geometric definition of the gap regions (@sec-mechanism,
@tbl-hilift-hlreg), against the physical-drive GeoTransolver. The
physical-drive error ratio at 35 cases is smallest in the gap regions
(2.0x against 3.0x on the open surfaces; 1.9x against 2.6x at 210), and
ISLA's own residual error concentrates there (59–71% of its squared error
on 15% of the points). The ratios are physical-drive measurements; the
ISLA-internal fact stands. The instrument finds where *output* error sits,
not where the *input* information that produces it lives, and at 35 cases
there is no error advantage to localize; the instrument is retained for any
rung at which the unit-drive reruns leave one.

**The remaining deficit is representational, not a shortage of training
cases.** The cleanest test of a data limit is to remove the data axis:
train each architecture on a single case, presented as 64 independent
10,000-cell views of the same surface, until its training loss stops
falling, and read the floor it reaches on a fresh resampling of that same
case (companion notebook, single-case study, 2026-09-11; float32; the
arms carry the unit-drive input, and the fp32-trained pair is the
like-for-like comparison). If the 35-case gap were a data limit, the gap
at one case should be smaller or vanish; it is wider. On the HiLiftAeroML
wing ISLA's single-case floor is 1.27x GeoTransolver's and 1.37x
Transolver's in the bfloat16-trained arms and 1.55x in the fp32-trained
pair, against a 35-case gap of 1.11–1.20x; on the DrivAerML car it is
1.31–1.39x, over the pre-registered 1.5x capacity bar in the fp32 pair.
The same ordering is visible in the training losses on ISLA's own
views, so the gap is present before any generalization question arises.
Two further facts locate it. With the data fixed, the weights-off
ablation still beats the reference by 17% on both datasets, so the
measure-weight cost measured on the ladder is not a few-sample effect
(it remains an ablation, @sec-principle). A forward-pass probe of the
trained single-case checkpoints identified its mechanism as estimator
variance, not saturation or starvation (companion notebook, routing
probe, 2026-09-11). Uniform-over-cells sampling draws a heavy tail of
cell areas (4.4% of the wing's cells carry half the sampled area), and a
quadrature-weighted mean over such a draw has an effective sample size
of $N/(1+\mathrm{CV}^2)$ of the areas: 862 of 9,983 wing cells, 1,637 of
10,000 car cells. The learned routing sits at that floor, so each slice
state with weights on is a mean over about one fifth as many effective
tokens as with weights off, and over four resamplings of the same
surface the slice states move 1.9–2.3x more relative to their spread,
while the number of distinct slice states is unchanged. No slice is
dominated by a few large cells (ten cells never carry more than 18% of a
slice's mass), and slices routed to large cells are not poorer in
tokens than others, so neither saturation nor open-surface starvation
holds. Split by facing distance, the deficit sits on the mid- and
far-field open surfaces (baseline-to-ISLA ratios 0.64–0.83) and is
smallest at the gaps (0.88), which is where a uniform noise floor shows
most: on the smooth regions where the residual is smallest and which
dominate the area-weighted metric of @sec-metrics. The principled target
is therefore the sampler or a variance-reduced consistent quadrature,
not the weights. The consistency benchmark of @sec-consistency-bench
already shows what the weights-off ablation learned instead. Evaluated
on the area-proportional sampler, where the quadrature weights are
nearly constant, the uniform-trained weights-off checkpoints do not
merely lose their 2–13% uniform-sampler advantage, they collapse: their
errors are 0.66–1.29 (worse than predicting zero) against 0.10–0.51 for
weights on, a 2–7x inversion on all three datasets, and weights-on's
error keeps falling with cell count while weights-off's stays flat
(`results/consistency_bench/consistency_bench_2026-09-10.json`, float32,
two seeds). Both checkpoints are scored off their training sampling law,
so this mixes the routing computation with what each set of parameters
learned to expect; the reading that fits is that the uniform-sampler
advantage is estimator variance plus mesh-pattern content, and the
mesh-pattern part dominates what weights-off learned. The two parts
separate by their dependence on cell count, because estimator variance
shrinks as more cells are drawn and mesh-pattern content does not. On
the uniform sampler the weights-off-to-weights-on ratio on DrivAerML
rises from 0.89 at 2,500 cells to 0.98 at 40,000, so the car advantage
behaves as variance and is nearly gone at the highest count; on
HiLiftAeroML at 35 cases (0.88) and on the fixed-angle split (0.87) the
ratio is flat across the same sixteen-fold range, which variance cannot
produce. On the wings, then, the ablation's advantage is mesh-pattern
content, and the wings are where its collapse under area sampling is
worst. The area-trained ISLA of the mixed-sampling study, run through
the same benchmark and read under the uniform sampler at 40,000 cells,
lands at the weights-on level (0.0591 against 0.0579 for its
uniform-trained twin; the weights-off arm scores 0.0518 against its own
twin's 0.0530), so training under the constant-weight law does not buy
back the advantage: the variance that matters on the cars is the
evaluation-time variance of the slice means, and it is removed by
drawing more cells, not by retraining (@sec-nb-mix-refinement). This is the program's rule in @sec-principle read from the data:
accuracy is to be recovered by capacity and principled construction, not
by tuning to a dataset, and the single-case floor is the instrument that
separates the two. The interior pair of the same study sorts ISLA's three
interior standings the same way (one car, 64 views, float32 at the
training count of 10,000 queries; @sec-nb-overfit-interior): against
GeoTransolver-volume the single-car ratios are 1.25 on pressure, 0.67 on
velocity and 1.64 on eddy viscosity, against 0.92, 0.65 and 1.30 at full
data. The velocity lead is identical with the data fixed, so it is
capacity; the eddy-viscosity deficit is wider with the data fixed, so it is
capacity too and more cars will not close it; and the full-data pressure
lead disappears on one car, so it is generalization across cars, not
representation.

### Regime extrapolation fails for every architecture tested {#sec-limits-regime}

**Neither architecture generalizes across a flow-regime boundary, and ISLA's
structure does not change that** (@sec-regime-extrapolation). The readout is
d = (pressure rel-L2 on the sealed out-of-regime test set) / (pressure rel-L2
on in-regime validation cases). Trained at angles of attack up to 12° and
tested at 14° and above, or trained pre-stall and tested post-stall, both
architectures lose about a factor of ten, and the out-of-regime errors
(0.24–0.33) are worse than either architecture reaches from 35 in-regime
cases (ISLA 0.138, unit-drive GeoTransolver 0.111–0.124). ISLA keeps the lower
absolute error against the physical-drive GeoTransolver, which has the
smaller d because its in-regime floor is higher; both GeoTransolver regime
lanes consumed the physical velocity (@sec-part-baseline), so the ordering
and the ratios are physical-drive measurements. Coverage of the regime, not
architecture, governs this axis.

Whether GeoTransolver's smaller ratio comes from its raw-coordinate inputs
was tested directly: ISLA with a raw-coordinate channel appended to its seed
invariants, which breaks the SE(3) contract, trained on the stall split with
two seeds and evaluated once on the sealed post-stall test. The
preregistered bands were: raw coordinates carry the ratio if d is 11.0 or
below with out-of-regime pressure below 0.245; they do not if d is 12.0 or
above or pressure is 0.255 or above. Measured: d = 12.7/13.3, against 12.5
for ISLA and 9.3 for GeoTransolver, with sealed-test pressure
0.262/0.267. The falsifier fires: raw-coordinate inputs do not give ISLA
GeoTransolver's smaller ratio, and no mechanism for it has been isolated.
Because ISLA has the lower absolute error on both sides of the boundary,
there is no transfer advantage to explain and the thread is closed.

### Interior accuracy: ahead on velocity with query tokens and the signed distance, behind on pressure and eddy viscosity; the passive decode trails by 2.6x {#sec-limits-interior}

**On the boundary → interior task, ISLA with query tokens and the signed
distance as an input is more accurate than GeoTransolver's volume
configuration on interior velocity (0.75x in float32, three seeds) and less
accurate on interior pressure (1.08x) and eddy viscosity (1.27x) at a third
of the parameters; at matched parameters (hidden 344, 27.6M) it leads on
pressure (0.97x) and velocity (0.68x) and trails on eddy viscosity (1.18x,
companion #sec-campaigns-interior); in bfloat16, which
inflates GeoTransolver-volume's errors by 20–23% and ISLA's by 4–7%, the
pressure ratio read 0.91x (@sec-nb-fp32-interior-regrade); without the
signed distance it trails on every field (1.19x, 1.28x, 1.61x in
float32); ISLA's passive, query-independent decode trails by 3.1x on
pressure (float32), and that
deficit grows with distance from the wall** (@sec-interior). The setting is
DrivAerML volume fields at 10,000 interior query points; ISLA predicts them
from 10,000 surface tokens, GeoTransolver from the interior points
themselves as interacting tokens carrying the signed distance to the wall,
at 27.6M parameters against ISLA's 8.9M. Three limits. GeoTransolver-volume
consumes the physical freestream velocity (38.9 m/s) where ISLA consumes the
unit direction, the same asymmetry that produced the baselines' HiLiftAeroML
deficit at a 69x larger magnitude (@sec-part-baseline); its unit-drive
rerun (@sec-nb-udrv-int-prereg) was null: pressure 0.0617, velocity 0.131,
eddy viscosity 0.0936 against 0.0620, 0.1334, 0.0939, all within the 3%
band (@sec-nb-udrv-int-verdict), so the interior ratios are not an
input-scale artifact. The
signed-distance
arm's preregistered pressure bar landed in its inconclusive band (an 11%
fall against 15% to count as supported), so its pressure gain is reported
as measured, not as a confirmed hypothesis; its velocity and
eddy-viscosity gains were anticipated but not given bars. And the
full-data statement only partly extends to small data: at 54 and 109
training cars GeoTransolver leads the query-token configuration without
the signed distance by a constant 1.2x on interior pressure, the same 1.2x
by which it leads ISLA on the DrivAerML surface below full data; with the
signed distance the pressure deficit is 1.11x at 54 cars and 1.06x at 109,
velocity is an ISLA advantage at every size (0.83x, 0.73x, 0.64x), and
eddy viscosity stays 1.3–1.5x in GeoTransolver's favour, so below full
data ISLA leads on velocity from 109 cars up and trails by 18–19% on
pressure in float32 (@sec-interior-open). The 3.1x is the cost of the complete passive
configuration as built, a separate four-block read decoder without the
signed-distance input, against a query-token configuration that routes its
queries through the twelve encoder blocks; what query independence alone
costs at matched depth and inputs is not yet measured
(@sec-program-status). For the passive decode, the deficit ratio is 2.5x
near the wall and 3.3–5.4x in the far bands, while 95% of the excess
squared error on the sampled points lies within 5 cm of the wall, so the
ratio's growth does not identify a missing mechanism
(@sec-interior-distance). In the passive configuration interior queries are
decoded passively; in the query-token configuration behind the interior
headline they are interacting tokens. The one attempt to supply interior
context while keeping the passive decode, equivariant latent
tokens placed off each slice anchor along its mean normal, made the interior
decode worse by 1.43x. An exact boundary-integral prior is not an option
either: on DrivAerML a potential-flow oracle scores worse than predicting each
case's mean pressure, because the dominant physics is separation
(@sec-interior-negatives). The open item on the interior is the
eddy-viscosity gap (1.29x at full data on the recipe's standardized
viscosity metric, which is not a physical percentage, flat across an
eightfold change in
training data with inputs matched): surface-patch local features on the
query tokens did not close it, and neither did a width increase to hidden
256 (1.17x in float32, inside the inconclusive band; 1.26x in bfloat16;
about 15.7M parameters, still
below GeoTransolver-volume's effective width of 448 and 27.6M parameters,
so capacity is not ruled out, only that step in width;
@sec-interior-query-tokens). The single-car test then identified it as a
capacity limit outright: with the data fixed the eddy-viscosity ratio widens
to 1.64, so more training cars will not close it
(@sec-nb-overfit-interior). Two facts bound
the query-token configuration itself: its query weights scale with the
geometric mean of the surface weights, so refining the surface sample or
changing the number of queries changes its prediction (4–9% on small random
models; on the trained checkpoint the advantage holds at or above the
training query count of 10,000 and is consumed below it,
@sec-interior-companion); and DrivAerML's hybrid RANS/LES closure makes the
modeled viscosity depend on the mesh, so a local aggregation over
neighbouring interior points may recover discretization rather than
physics; giving ISLA the local query density or a neighbour channel
directly did not close the eddy-viscosity gap (@sec-interior-open), which
weakens that reading without settling it.

### Exact query independence costs 3.0–3.7x and is not in the reference configuration {#sec-limits-query-independence}

**ISLA's surface predictions in the reference configuration depend weakly on
which other points are sampled; making them exactly independent costs
3.0–3.7x in accuracy, so every surface checkpoint behind the headline
results is the interacting configuration** (@sec-query-independence). Query
independence means the prediction at a point does not change when the other
queried points change. In the reference configuration the heads read from
the interacting encoder tokens, and swapping the companion set moves a
point's prediction by about 7% (2% for GeoTransolver at a shared 5,000-cell
prefix). The optional query-independent configuration replaces the heads
with passive read blocks; it is exactly independent in fp64 and 3.0–3.7x
less accurate on DrivAerML surface pressure: 3.5–3.7x against the
interacting reference at the same learning rate, 3.0–3.3x against the
6,500-token control at matched memory.
Evaluate-anywhere semantics is a contract with a measured price. The
interior confirms it at matched depth: a passive decode that reads through
twelve blocks from an interacting support set of 5,000 surface-plus-signed-
distance tokens (the companion's D1 arm) scores 0.078 / 0.107 / 0.269 on
pressure, velocity and eddy viscosity against 0.055 / 0.080 / 0.112 for the
interacting query-token reference, 1.43x, 1.34x and 2.41x, far past the
preregistered falsifier of 0.060 on pressure; depth buys 13% and the support
12% on pressure and neither anything on eddy viscosity. What the interacting
queries provide is computation at the requested points through every
encoder layer, not geometric context, so the passive route is closed for
ISLA at matched depth and inputs
(`research/transfer_program/studies/computational_support/d1_verdict_2026-09-10.json`, companion #sec-computational-support).
Training over a range of request sizes reduces the dependence by about 40%
at a 3.7% accuracy cost and does not remove it (@sec-nb-qcount-verdict), so
the interacting decode's request-size dependence is partly intrinsic, and
deployment at the training count remains the rule.

### Cross-family transfer is a data property {#sec-limits-transfer}

**Neither ISLA nor GeoTransolver transfers zero-shot across vehicle
families; what moves cross-family error is the diversity of the training
data** (@tbl-frontier in @sec-full-data). The failure is not identical across
the two architectures — on the held-out fastback family the reference
configurations trained on DrivAerML alone score, in float32 on two seeds,
0.61 for the unit-drive GeoTransolver and 0.79 for ISLA (0.98 for ISLA's
constant-gauge configuration; 1.0 is the mean predictor), so ISLA's
zero-shot failure is 29% worse than GeoTransolver's — but neither is usable,
and a second training family moves both to 0.11–0.13. Few-shot adaptation separates them further: fine-tuned on 20
labelled fastback cases for 1,000 steps, the unit-drive GeoTransolver
reaches 0.128 against 0.186 trained from scratch on those cases, while ISLA
reaches 0.187 against 0.198 (float32, matched learning rate;
research/transfer_program, #sec-nb-campc-t3-verdict), so what GeoTransolver
learns on DrivAerML is a better starting point for a new family than what
ISLA learns there (the two source checkpoints differ in drive input and
learning rate as well as architecture, a caveat stated with the result).
That the ISLA fine-tune started from its trained weights was checked
directly after a checkpoint-loading hazard surfaced (#sec-nb-snapshot-resolved):
the source model passed through the fine-tuning loader at zero learning rate
reproduces its own zero-shot error to four digits (0.9791 both ways). The
cleanest form of the finding is at the two ends of adaptation: on the first
batch of fastback cases the pretrained ISLA's training loss is 2.5x lower
than a random initialization's (0.194 against 0.477) and the pretrained
GeoTransolver's 1.6x lower (0.176 against 0.278), so the two architectures'
DrivAerML knowledge is worth about the same at step zero; after 1,000
matched-rate steps ISLA's head start has shrunk to 6% while GeoTransolver's
has grown to 31%. No single ISLA ingredient carries that deficit: retraining
with 128 or 512 anchors, with raw seeds in place of the drive-relative
invariants, with the similarity gauge at either rate or with the measure weights off
moves the zero-shot fastback error nowhere near GeoTransolver's (best arm
0.767 against 0.788 and 0.612; three seeds each, spreads up to 0.30;
@sec-nb-xfam-verdict), so the cross-family question is a data question,
which is where campaign C's diversity results place it. Diversity at a fixed label budget is a trade, not a free
lunch: with 435 training cases split 218 DrivAerML and 217 estate instead of
all DrivAerML, ISLA's zero-shot fastback error falls from 0.788 to 0.128 and
GeoTransolver's from 0.612 to 0.115 (drag error from above 150% to 16% and
13%), while in-family DrivAerML error rises from 0.0557 to 0.0737 for ISLA
(+32%) and from 0.0504 to 0.0598 for GeoTransolver (+19%) (float32, seed
means; `research/transfer_program/studies/campaign_c_transfer/campaign_c_t2_2026-09-10.json`,
#sec-nb-campc-t2-verdict). The preregistered bar, a 30% drop at no more than
10% in-family cost, fails on the cost side for both architectures. Four
protocol-matched lanes trained on the 218 DrivAerML cars alone split the
cost: for ISLA, halving the source data costs 1.23x (0.0557 to 0.0683) and
adding the 217 estate cars on top costs a further 1.08x (to 0.0737); for
GeoTransolver the factors are 1.14x and 1.04x. Most of the in-family cost
is therefore what any halving of the source data costs, the sibling family
itself costs 4–8% at a 50% share, and ISLA pays more on both factors, in the
same direction as the few-shot result (#tbl-campc-t2-decomp). At a fixed
label budget, half the labels on the target's sibling family buy the target
family almost entirely and cost the source about what halving its data
costs, plus 4–8% for the mixing. Two further facts from the same campaign
bound the trade. The mixing cost grows with the foreign share for ISLA and
not for GeoTransolver: with all 435 DrivAerML cars kept and 794 estate cars
added (a 65% foreign share, source not halved) ISLA's in-family error rises
17% (0.0557 to 0.0652) and GeoTransolver's 4% (0.0504 to 0.0525), against 8%
and 4% at the 50% share; and the extra 577 estate cars buy the fastback
cases only 6% (ISLA) and 9% (GeoTransolver) over the 217-car mix, so
coverage of a sibling family saturates within a few hundred cars. A per-case
family flag (a boundary scalar for ISLA, a seventh functional channel for
GeoTransolver) changes nothing on the held-out family or in-family (within
the seed spread), so the mismatch is coverage, not identification
(`research/transfer_program/studies/campaign_c_transfer/campaign_c_t1_2026-09-10.json`,
companion #sec-campaigns-conditioning). With the zero-shot force error
of 1.6x and the constant-gauge density collapse, this is the third
independent sign that ISLA's learned representation is family-specific. The similarity
gauge, which fixes the constant-gauge configuration's sampling-density
failure (@sec-robustness-density), leaves zero-shot transfer unchanged. A claim of family-portable surface physics from any of these
architectures would need a corpus in which geometry, pose, scale and regime
vary one at a time (@sec-open-questions).

## Open questions, and what would settle each {#sec-open-questions}

Each question has, or acquires before it runs, a preregistered prediction
in readout units and a
falsifier,^[Preregistrations: @sec-nb-udrvl-prereg, @sec-nb-udrv-int-prereg,
@sec-nb-w2-prereg, @sec-nb-deflection-prereg, @sec-nb-qt-h256-prereg,
@sec-nb-g5-prereg, @sec-nb-mom2-prereg.] and
none is yet measured (@sec-program-status). Unless stated, the readout is the
pressure rel-L2 of @sec-limits-data-efficiency and the ratio is baseline ÷
ISLA, so above 1 favours ISLA; the older preregistrations were written in
ISLA/GT, the inverse, and each threshold below is labelled with its
direction. The first two questions are the ones whose answers would most
change the book: they decide whether ISLA has any accuracy advantage
anywhere once the inputs are matched.

- **Does ISLA have an accuracy advantage at any HiLiftAeroML rung against
  unit-drive baselines?** GeoTransolver fed the unit freestream direction at
  210 and 1,260 training cases and on the 4- and 21-geometry rungs, and
  Transolver at 210 cases, with the frozen protocol and the reference lanes'
  learning rates (@sec-nb-udrvl-prereg). At each rung, ISLA has an advantage
  only if baseline ÷ ISLA is at least 1.10 with ISLA lower on at least two
  thirds of the validation cases (and on at least 12 of 18 geometries on the
  geometry rungs); parity is 0.95–1.05; the baseline is ahead at 0.90 or
  below, as at 35 cases (0.90 GeoTransolver, 0.83 Transolver). Prediction:
  the unit-drive baselines match or beat ISLA at every rung. Measured at
  six of seven rungs, the prediction holds: GeoTransolver 0.83x at 210 cases
  (Transolver 0.91x), 0.84x at 510 cases (Transolver 0.90x; both lower on 168
  of 180 cases), 0.76x at 4 geometries, 0.92x at 21 geometries, 0.78x at
  the fixed angle (@sec-nb-udrvl-210-verdict, @sec-nb-udrvl-510-verdict,
  @sec-nb-udrvl-geo210-verdict,
  @sec-nb-udrvl-geo40-verdict, @sec-nb-udrv-single-verdict); the 2.2x, 1.8x,
  1.4x and 5.0x were physical-drive measurements (@sec-part-baseline); the
  1,260-case rerun is the one still training.
- **If an advantage survives at some rung, where on the wing does it
  live, and is gap geometry the information that carries it?** The
  gap-distance stratification of @sec-mechanism, re-run against the
  unit-drive checkpoints at that rung (localization: supported if the
  near-gap-band ratio is at least 1.5x the rest-of-surface ratio, falsified
  if uniform within 1.15x), followed by a perturbation test (gap-region
  points removed or perturbed against matched-area controls on a fixed
  query set) for the information question. Both are conditional on the
  first question leaving something to explain; against the physical-drive
  GeoTransolver the localization read the other way (@sec-limits-mechanism).
- **Is the flattening a protocol floor?** Both architectures at 1,260 cases
  with 20,000 rather than 10,000 sampled points per case. If the floor is
  the protocol's, both improve by a similar factor (within 5 percentage
  points). If GeoTransolver improves by 10 percentage points or more than
  ISLA, the floor is ISLA's. The GeoTransolver arm is a physical-drive lane;
  its reading is about the floor, not the ordering.
- **The 510-case rung and the deflection split** were launched with
  physical-drive GeoTransolver arms (bars in @sec-nb-w2-prereg and
  @sec-nb-deflection-prereg, written in ISLA/GT); the 510-case rung has
  since been re-measured with unit-drive baselines, which lead ISLA 0.84x and
  0.90x (@sec-nb-udrvl-510-verdict). Their ISLA arms are kept
  as measurements of ISLA's curve between 210 and 1,260 cases and across a
  geometry-parameter boundary (the 80% of geometries with the lower
  flap-and-slat deflection to the 20% with the most aggressive settings, one
  sealed evaluation; held out per checkpoint, not a program-level
  confirmation, @sec-limits-validation); neither is a comparison of
  architectures unless a unit-drive baseline is run on the same split.
- **The query-token prediction depends on the query cloud, and the
  dependence is measured** (@sec-interior-companion): on the trained
  query-token model with the signed distance, the pressure error at 1,000
  fixed points is 0.062 when they are queried with 9,000 companions (the
  training count), 0.077 with 1,000, 0.110 alone, and 0.056 with 39,000;
  the passive configuration's dependence is exactly zero in fp32. The
  0.005 advantage over GeoTransolver-volume therefore exists at or above the
  training query count and is consumed below it. Open: whether training
  with a range of query counts, or the measure-consistent query-mass
  convention (@sec-mt2-contracts), removes the dependence; and whether ISLA
  with the intended 10,000 surface tokens rather than the 365 it received
  (@sec-interior-task) changes any interior number (V0-SURF10K,
  @sec-nb-v0surf-prereg).
- **What does query independence itself cost on the interior?** ISLA with
  the queries routed through the same twelve encoder blocks as in the
  query-token configuration, with the signed distance, but with their writes
  into the shared slice state disabled, so that depth, readout and inputs
  are held fixed and only interaction is removed. Falsified as a fundamental
  cost if this configuration is within 1.3x of GeoTransolver-volume on
  interior pressure (the 3.1x was the complete passive configuration);
  confirmed as a cost of interaction if it stays at 2.0x or more.
- **What is the force error against the full surface?** Lift and drag
  from 10,000, 20,000 and 40,000 sampled cells and from the full surface,
  labels and predictions, on a preselected set of validation cases at 35 and
  1,260 training cases. ISLA's 3% figure at 35 cases holds against the full
  surface if the full-surface error is within 1.5 percentage points of the
  sampled-cell error; if the sampled-cell reference itself deviates from the
  full-surface integral by more than the model error, the reported force
  errors are quadrature-limited and are restated against the full surface.
  The baselines' 35-case force errors in @sec-data-efficiency (8–17%) are
  physical-drive measurements; the unit-drive baselines' forces are not yet
  reduced.
- **Is a second-moment channel worth having?** The expressivity benchmark
  on the first-moment collision family (@sec-mt2-contracts): ISLA with a
  per-slice second-moment contraction, against the base model and the
  local-distance channel, scored by whether a linear probe on the
  common-component output separates the two arrangement families; bars in
  @sec-nb-mom2-prereg. It decides whether the documented representation
  limitation is cheap to remove before any larger geometric-algebra backbone
  is considered.
- **Is there a stronger independent baseline?** Every baseline in this
  book is from the Transolver family. AB-UPT (an anchored neural-field
  decoder; TMLR, arXiv 2502.09692) is the published architecture whose
  design most directly contradicts the interior finding here, that
  accuracy needed the queries to interact; AB-GATr (arXiv 2605.18816) is
  the scalable equivariant comparator for ISLA's combination of symmetry
  and accuracy; regularized family adaptation (arXiv 2605.27968) tests
  whether the zero-shot cross-family failure is cheaper to close by
  adapting than by collecting a family from scratch; and Transolver++ is
  the template's `plus` option, a cheap control that is not a reproduction
  of that paper. Each is a candidate node, to be run under this protocol
  with the freestream at unit scale for every model; published numbers
  on other splits are not a comparison with ISLA.
- **Does boundary self-identification help ISLA?** The largest measured
  industrial gain of the exact-kernel MeshTransformer (@sec-interior) came from a trace
  formulation that let each boundary token identify its own cell in the
  readout, so that a prediction at a surface point had an explicit term from
  that point's own cell rather than only from the pooled field. ISLA's
  routing has no analogous explicit term: the heads read each surface
  point's encoder token, but after twelve layers of slice routing that token
  holds whatever the routing mixed into it, and nothing in the readout marks
  the point's own position, normal and area apart from the field. The test
  is a single-factor addition of an own-token readout channel to ISLA,
  everything else frozen, at 35 and 1,260 HiLift cases, two seeds. Falsified
  if it moves neither rung by more than the two-seed spread; a gain at 35
  cases only would say the term is a small-data aid, at both rungs that
  ISLA's readout is missing a general ingredient.
- **Which generalization axes does structure buy, one at a time?** A 3D
  RANS corpus generated with counterfactual twin draws per factor (pose,
  scale, Reynolds number, layout, mesh), so each axis is tested exactly.
  Preregistered: on pose twins GeoTransolver without a freestream frame
  fails by 5x or more and canonicalized GeoTransolver matches ISLA within
  1.05x; on scale twins at fixed Reynolds number across 0.02–20 m (the
  first real test of the similarity gauge) GeoTransolver exceeds 2x at a 10x
  scale change; on Reynolds twins no architecture transfers a decade of Re
  better than another; mesh twins set the floor below which no difference
  is reportable. The arms are void unless twin draws are adopted at
  generation time, which is why the preregistration precedes the corpus.

## Engineering directions {#sec-future}

**Memory headroom.** On one GB300 with one instrument, ISLA's current
code peaks at 1.6 GiB of training memory at 10,000 tokens against
GeoTransolver's 4.1 GiB, 2.6x less, while the ISLA code that trained every
checkpoint in this book peaked at 9.3 GiB, 2.3x more; ISLA's step is 3.7x
slower (results/matched_memory_isla_gt_2026-09-08.json; @sec-mt2-cost).^[Measurement
records: @sec-nb-geo-pool-memory, @sec-nb-geo-recompute.] Two exact
rewrites set the current figure. The relational readback pools the
softmax slice mixture before the affine projection, so the activation
saved per layer for the backward pass is (points × 8) rather than
(points × slices × hidden/2), and the remaining per-slice geometry is
rebuilt inside the backward pass rather than stored (2.3x less memory for
1.16x step time); the rewrites compute the same function
(fp64 maximum difference 4e-15). Fusing that recompute region with the
compiler recovers the step time and more (0.82x the eager stored path, at
1.28 GiB), but rounds the bf16 chain differently, so it is a validated speed
option rather than part of the frozen protocol (@sec-nb-geo-compile). The
gap below GeoTransolver's footprint is real headroom for more tokens per
case or a wider model, at 3.7x GeoTransolver's step time; no accuracy
number in this book was produced at the smaller footprint. The
20,000-token floor test is affordable on ISLA's own measured numbers
(2.78 GiB).

**Measure weights: a training-time cost and an inference-time gain.** ISLA
weights each surface point by its cell area in the slice routing and the
pooled anchors. Under uniform 10,000-point sampling the weights are a source
of gradient variance rather than information: turning them off improves the
35-case error by 12% (0.88x). With the similarity gauge on, they are also
what make ISLA insensitive to sampling density at inference: ISLA with the
similarity gauge degrades 1.20x under a 10:1 biased density on DrivAerML,
against 3.6x for GeoTransolver (@sec-robustness-density). That is not the
configuration behind any accuracy number in this book: the similarity gauge
costs 8% at 35 cases, and the constant-gauge configuration behind every
accuracy result degrades 13–14.5x under the same bias, worse than
GeoTransolver. The trade has not been measured as a trade; training without
weights and evaluating under biased density would put the cost and the gain
on one table.

**Area-proportional sampling, untested.** Sampling points with probability
proportional to cell area, so that every sampled point carries equal measure
and the explicit weights become uniform, would remove the gradient-variance
cost while preserving the measure semantics of the routing. It moves density
robustness from the model to the sampler, which is acceptable in training
and a liability at inference if the query cloud is not under the model's
control. It is not yet measured (@sec-program-status).

## What would change the recommendation {#sec-review-roads}

ISLA is not recommended over GeoTransolver for HiLiftAeroML surface
pressure: at the one rung where the inputs have been matched, 35 training
cases, GeoTransolver and Transolver fed the unit direction are 1.1–1.25x
more accurate (1.07–1.11x against the weights-off ablation), and at every other rung the comparison is a physical-drive
measurement awaiting its rerun (@sec-part-baseline). On smooth single-body
families such as DrivAerML, GeoTransolver is 1.2–1.3x more accurate on the
surface below full data (physical drive, which on this dataset is not a
handicap) and 8–10% more accurate at full data in float32 (5–7% for the weights-off ablation, which is not adopted); GeoTransolver or Transolver is the
recommendation on DrivAerML at every size. Where geometries arrive in arbitrary poses the contracts earn accuracy: on
DrivAerML with every training and validation case in its own random SO(3)
pose, ISLA scores 0.0566 (1.01x its canonical error) against 0.0602 for
GeoTransolver with SO(3) augmentation (1.20x its canonical) and 0.0676 for
Transolver with augmentation (1.31x), a 6% and 19% lead in float32 that
reverses the canonical-frame ordering (research/transfer_program,
#sec-nb-campb-verdict); augmentation recovers only 4 of GeoTransolver's 25
lost points. Elsewhere what ISLA offers on the surface is its contracts:
exact rotation and translation covariance without a frame estimate or a
freestream direction at inference, which a canonicalized GeoTransolver
matches only where a frame can be estimated (@sec-pose); a
query-independent configuration at a measured 3.0–3.7x accuracy cost
(@sec-query-independence); and, with the similarity gauge on, insensitivity
to sampling density at inference: 1.21x under a 10:1 bias in float32 against
9.5x for the unit-drive GeoTransolver and 3.9x for Transolver
(@tbl-consistency-matrix, @sec-robustness-density). That last column is the
one the recommendation has to be read with (@sec-principle), and it splits
the recommendation. On accuracy the baselines lead: with the surface
measure in their slice pooling GeoTransolver and Transolver keep their
in-distribution lead on both datasets (0.0498 and 0.0522 on DrivAerML;
0.85x and 0.88x of ISLA at 35 HiLift cases; @sec-nb-mw-verdict). On
consistency the frame decides, not the pooling: every architecture that
centres its coordinates on a plain sample mean collapses under the 10:1
bias when the frame is taken from the biased sample (weighted baselines
14–16x, unweighted 12x, constant-gauge ISLA 12x; @sec-nb-mw-postcenter),
and only ISLA's measure-weighted frames hold (1.17–1.21x). Given an
unbiased estimate of the geometric centroid as their datapipe frame, the
measure-weighted baselines hold too: retrained with an area-weighted
centre they score 0.0505 and 0.0528 (within 1.2% of their plain-frame
twins) and their sample-frame density ratio is 1.04x and 1.03x when the
centre is the Horvitz–Thompson estimate of the geometric centroid, against
9.2x and 6.0x when it is the raw-area mean (@sec-nb-mwaw-verdict;
`results/mwaw_2026-09-11.json`). The consistency advantage is therefore a
property of the frame, not of the architecture. So on surface
pressure at the reference size the measure-weighted GeoTransolver or
Transolver is the more accurate choice wherever the deployment mesher
matches the training mesher, and ISLA is the choice wherever the sampling
may differ, where geometries arrive in arbitrary poses, on the interior at
matched parameters, or where memory at scale binds. The measure-weighted,
Horvitz–Thompson-centred GeoTransolver and Transolver that match ISLA on
consistency are research variants built for this comparison, to locate the
property in the frame rather than in the architecture; the released
GeoTransolver and Transolver are stable, in use and published, and will
not be modified (ruling of 2026-09-11), so measure weighting and the
geometric frame reach users through ISLA. The fair comparison therefore
reports the released baselines as the deployable comparison and their
measure-consistent variants as the diagnostic. Under
refinement and across sampling laws no configuration is yet consistent at
10,000 cells; only the measure-weighted ISLA arms converge toward the
uniform answer under the area-proportional sampler while the unweighted
baselines are flat (@sec-consistency-bench), and whether the weighted
baselines converge too is being measured. Trained on one sampling
convention and deployed on another, every architecture pays at 10,000
cells, ISLA with measure weights 1.5–1.9x and the baselines 3–7x, and every
architecture trained on both conventions handles both at no cost
(@sec-nb-mix-verdict). For the measure-weighted ISLA that penalty is a
finite-sample effect and it converges: trained under one convention and
scored under the other, the ratio falls from 2.9x at 2,500 cells to 1.45x
at 10,000 and 1.05x at 40,000 (the reverse direction 2.7x to 1.21x),
while the unweighted baselines' 3–7x does not move
(@sec-nb-mix-refinement;
`results/consistency_bench/consistency_bench_mixarea_2026-09-11.json`).
Mesher transfer is a property of the training data at this resolution,
and of the measure-consistent estimator in the fine-mesh limit, which at
40,000 cells is within 5% of reached. Which frame ISLA stands on is decided (2026-09-11): the frame-free
construction (RELFRAME, no centroid anywhere) keeps the constant gauge's
accuracy on DrivAerML at the same 1.2x density floor as the other
measure-consistent frames, which is therefore the routing integral's own
variance and not a frame effect, and is consistent under every sampler on
both datasets (@sec-nb-relframe-hl-bench), but pays 11% at 35 HiLift cases exactly
as the measure-centred frame did, so that price is not frame variance
either (@sec-nb-relframe-verdict); the full-geometry-frame diagnostic
decided what it is: given the exact geometric frame and every positional
seed, ISLA pays 14–16% on the wings, so the price is the mesh-density
content of the plain-mean frame (0.13 body lengths), and by the
preregistered rule the reference configuration is the relative frame with
the total-measure scale, which pays that 11% for carrying no mesher
information (@sec-nb-frame-full-verdict). The first rung of the ladder
that trains the reference on the remaining splits supports the reading
that the mesher pattern pays only where validation geometries recur in
training: on 4 training geometries, validated on 18 never-seen geometries,
the reference scores 0.2520 against the constant-gauge prior's 0.2496,
parity inside the seed spread where the preregistration had predicted a
5–10% price (@sec-nb-relframe-ladder-geo4). The fixed-angle rung then
showed that reading to be incomplete: it is also a never-seen-geometry
split, yet the reference pays 10% there (0.0384 against 0.0348, 18
geometries, two seeds; @sec-nb-relframe-ladder-fixed-angle), so on that
rung the two candidates from 35 cases remain open, the plain mean's mesher
pattern and the positional seeds at a fixed drive direction, and a
full-geometry-frame pair on the fixed-angle split is the experiment that
would separate them. The same rung settled the scale question the other
way from its hypothesis: the reference with the total-measure scale pays
less than the relative frame with a constant reference length (10% against
26%, the latter with a 22% seed spread), so normalizing away absolute size
is not the fixed-angle cost and the total-measure scale stands without a
caveat. Its learning-rate robustness is
measured against a physical-drive GeoTransolver and is not claimed as an
advantage until re-measured. On the interior, ISLA with query tokens and
the signed distance leads GeoTransolver's volume configuration on velocity
(0.75x in float32, three seeds) at a third of the parameters and trails on
pressure (1.08x) and eddy viscosity (1.27x), while at matched parameters it
leads on pressure as well (0.97x) and trails only on eddy viscosity (1.18x),
at or above the training query count
(@sec-interior); the unit-drive control of GeoTransolver-volume changed
nothing (@sec-nb-udrv-int-verdict), and GeoTransolver-volume is the choice
where pressure or eddy viscosity is the target field or the
training set is small and pressure is the target. Three outcomes would
change this.

**ISLA regains an accuracy claim on HiLiftAeroML** if the unit-drive
reruns leave it ahead at some rung by the preregistered margin (baseline ÷
ISLA at least 1.10 with ISLA lower on two thirds of the cases and 12 of 18
geometries on the geometry rungs; @sec-nb-udrvl-prereg). That rung and its
mechanism would then be the program's only accuracy claim, stated against
the unit-drive baseline, and the localization and perturbation instruments
of @sec-open-questions would run there. The prediction is that this does
not happen.

**The interior recommendation becomes unconditional for ISLA** only if
query-to-query local aggregation, the one
GeoTransolver-volume ingredient not yet transplanted, closes the
eddy-viscosity gap (within 1.10x) at the reference width without moving
pressure or velocity by more than 5% (the width increase to 256 moved it
to 1.17x in float32, inconclusive).

**The contracts become the whole case** if both controls read as
predicted: the program's ISLA-specific claims are then exact covariance,
the passive query-independent decode, the similarity gauge's density
robustness and the cost figures of @sec-mt2-cost, each with its measured
price, and no accuracy claim. If none of these fires, the recommendation
stands as written, with the bounds of this chapter attached.
